unit.title: Mark off/out structural fabrication and shapes

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What should you check before marking out a part from a drawing?
options: The drawing number, revision, sizes and material against the job card
Only the overall length, because the other sizes can be worked out later
The colour of paint the job will get, so the marks can be seen
Nothing, because the drawing has already been checked in the office

questions.stem: Why should the steel be checked for size, straightness and damage before marking out?
options: So you can tell the supplier to collect it again
So the marks will be easier to see on the surface
So time is not wasted marking material that cannot be used
So the steel can be painted before it is marked

questions.stem: How should a long steel section be supported for marking out?
options: Across two loose blocks of wood on the floor, near the door
On firm trestles, chocked so it cannot roll
Leaning against the wall at an angle
Held on one person's shoulder while another marks it

questions.stem: What is the main hazard when handling newly sheared or cut plate for marking out?
options: The plate may be magnetic and pull tools towards it
The plate will still be too hot to touch for days
The marking blue gives off a dangerous gas
Sharp edges and burrs that can cut the hands

questions.stem: When using a centre punch and hammer, which PPE is most needed?
options: Ear muffs only, because of the noise
A welding helmet with a dark filter
Safety glasses, because chips can fly off
A dust mask, because of the steel dust

questions.stem: Which marking tool is best for lines on rusty or hot plate that is to be flame cut?
options: Soapstone (French chalk)
A sharp pencil
Marking blue and a scriber
A ballpoint pen

questions.stem: What is a scriber used for?
options: Making a dent so that a drill starts in the right place
Measuring the thickness of plate and sheet
Drawing large circles on plate
Scratching fine, lasting lines on clean metal

questions.stem: What is marking blue (layout fluid) used for?
options: Stopping the steel from rusting after it is cut
Coating bright metal so that scribed lines show up clearly
Showing where the steel is too hot to touch
Cleaning oil and grease off the plate before welding

questions.stem: What is the difference between a dot (prick) punch and a centre punch?
options: A dot punch makes the big dent for drilling; a centre punch makes light marks
A dot punch makes light marks; a centre punch makes a bigger dent for drilling
A dot punch is used on wood; a centre punch is used on steel
There is no difference; the two names mean the same tool

questions.stem: Which tool marks a long straight line across a large plate?
options: A short steel rule, moved along a bit at a time
A small square, slid along the edge of the plate
A chalk line, pulled tight and snapped
A tape measure, held by one end only

questions.stem: Which tool scribes large arcs and circles, such as a 1.5 m circle on plate?
options: Trammels (a beam compass)
A small spring bow compass
An engineer's square
A centre punch and hammer

questions.stem: Why should you check the hook on the end of a tape measure before use?
options: A shiny hook reflects light and hides the marks
The hook is used to scribe the lines on the plate
A missing hook makes the tape roll back too slowly
A loose or bent hook gives wrong readings

questions.stem: Which tool finds the centre of the end of a round bar?
options: A spirit level and rule
A set of feeler gauges and a rule
A tape and soapstone
A centre head (centre square)

questions.stem: What is a datum in marking out?
options: A line or edge that all the measurements are taken from
The date the job was marked out, written on the plate
The last mark made on the job before cutting
The thickness of the plate, written on the drawing

questions.stem: Why are all hole positions measured from one datum and not from hole to hole?
options: It uses less marking blue and fewer scribed lines
The holes can then be any size you like
Small errors do not add up along the job
It makes the job quicker to paint

questions.stem: Before using a plate edge as a datum, what must you check?
options: That it has been painted
That it is straight and square
That it is the longest and widest edge
That it faces the window

questions.stem: A rectangle is marked out 1200 mm × 900 mm. If it is square, what should each diagonal measure?
Using the 3-4-5 rule, you mark 3 m along one line and 4 m along the other from the corner. What distance between the two marks gives a right angle?
options: 6 m
7 m
5 m

questions.stem: How can you mark a line at 90° to a straight edge using only trammels, a rule and a scriber?
options: Draw it by eye, then check it with a tape measure
Measure 90 mm along the edge and join it to the corner
Strike arcs from two points on the edge and join where they cross
Snap a chalk line from one corner of the plate to the opposite one

questions.stem: How do you find the centre of a large circular plate?
options: Measure across it once and halve that distance
Bisect two chords; the bisectors cross at the centre
Balance it on a pipe, and mark where it balances best
Mark the middle of the longest edge you can find

questions.stem: Six holes are to be evenly spaced on a 200 mm pitch circle. What distance do you step off round the circle to mark them?
options: 200 mm, the diameter
100 mm, the radius
33 mm, one sixth of 200 mm
60 mm, the angle in degrees

questions.stem: How many degrees apart are 8 holes evenly spaced on a pitch circle?
Why are witness marks (a ring of dots or a circle) put around a hole centre?
options: To make the hole easier to drill without using a pilot drill
To show which person marked out the hole
To show after drilling if the hole is in the right place
To stop the drill from slipping across the plate

questions.stem: In steelwork, what is the pitch of bolt holes?
options: The diameter of each bolt hole
The distance from a hole to the edge of the flange
The size of the bolt thread
The centre-to-centre distance between holes in a line

questions.stem: On a steel angle, what is the back mark (gauge line)?
options: The mark on the back of the angle that shows its size
The cut line marked across the end of the angle
The paint mark that shows the job number
The distance from the back of the angle to the hole line

questions.stem: Holes in a row start 40 mm from the end, with 4 holes at 75 mm pitch. How far is the last hole from the end?
options: 265 mm
340 mm
300 mm
225 mm

questions.stem: What does 100 × 75 × 8 unequal angle mean?
options: 100 mm long, 75 mm wide and 8 m in length
Legs of 100 mm and 75 mm, and 8 mm thick
A 100 mm leg with 75 holes of 8 mm
100 kg per metre, 75 mm wide, 8 mm thick

questions.stem: Which steel section is shaped like a capital I or H?
options: An equal or unequal angle
A parallel flange channel
A universal beam or column
A flat or square bar

questions.stem: How is a square cut line marked all the way round a channel or beam?
options: Square from one datum face and carry the line round each face
Mark one face only and cut the rest by eye
Wrap a chalk line right round it and snap it on each of the faces
Mark the top and bottom, then guess the web

questions.stem: How can you mark a square cut line around a pipe?
options: Measure from the end in one place only and mark a single dot
Hold a steel rule along the pipe and draw a line
Snap a chalk line along the pipe's length
Wrap a flexible strip tightly round and mark its edge

questions.stem: How are the quarter lines (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°) found on a pipe for a mitre or branch?
options: By guessing four points spaced by eye round the pipe
By measuring the outside diameter and marking it four times
By measuring round the pipe and dividing it into four
By rolling the pipe and marking where it stops

questions.stem: Two lengths of angle are joined at a 90° corner with a mitre. At what angle is each end cut?
Why are templates used when marking out?
options: To make the steel stronger before it is cut
To mark many identical parts quickly and accurately
To protect the plate surface from sparks during cutting
So that a drawing is not needed for the job

questions.stem: Before a template is used on steel, what should be done?
options: Paint it the same colour as the steel
Cut it slightly bigger than the drawing to allow for errors
Check it against the drawing and label it
Leave it in the sun to dry and harden

questions.stem: What is a development (stretch-out) in sheet and plate work?
options: The flat shape that folds or rolls into the finished part
A drawing of the finished part in isometric view
The extra metal added to a job for welding
A list of every part needed for the job

questions.stem: Which development method is used for a pipe cut at an angle, such as a mitre?
options: Radial line development
Triangulation
Isometric projection drawing
Parallel line development

questions.stem: Which development method is used for a cone, or a tapered hopper whose sides meet at a point?
options: Parallel line development
Triangulation
Radial line development
Orthographic projection

questions.stem: Which method is used to develop a square-to-round transition piece?
options: Triangulation
Parallel line development
Radial line development
Oblique projection

questions.stem: Why must you allow for the kerf when marking parts that will be flame cut?
options: The kerf makes the cut edge much harder to grind smooth later
The kerf changes the colour of the steel
The kerf adds metal to the edge of the part
The cut removes metal, so the part can end up undersize

questions.stem: When marking a plate that will be rolled into a cylinder, which diameter is used to work out its length?
options: The outside diameter
The mean (middle) diameter
The inside diameter
The diameter plus twice the thickness

questions.stem: Why should you look straight down at the rule when making a mark?
options: So the light does not shine into your eyes
So the rule does not slip on the plate
Looking from the side puts the mark in the wrong place
So that you can read the small numbers on the rule more easily

questions.stem: How should a marked-out job be checked before it is cut?
options: Look at it from across the workshop
Ask the person cutting to check it while they are cutting
Measure only the overall length once
Re-measure from the datum and compare with the drawing

questions.stem: Why are part marks and job numbers painted on marked-out pieces?
options: So each piece can be found and fitted in the right place
So the paint protects the steel from rust in storage
So the pieces look neat for the customer
So the pieces can be sold if they are not used

questions.stem: You find a size on the drawing that does not add up with the other sizes. What should you do?
options: Use the size that looks closest and carry on
Stop and ask the supervisor to check it before marking
Change the drawing yourself to make it add up
Mark it exactly as drawn and let the welder sort it out later

questions.stem: What should be done with marking-out tools at the end of the job?
options: Leave them on the plate ready for the next day
Put them in a bucket with the welding rods
Clean them, cover sharp points and put them away
Hang them on the trestles so they are easy to find

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe how you plan a marking-out job from a structural steel drawing, including the checks on the drawing, the material and the tools.
essays.modelAnswer: Read the drawing fully: the title block, the revision, the scale, the views, the sizes, the hole details and the notes. Check that it is the latest issue and that the sizes add up, and ask the supervisor about anything that is not clear. Make or check the cutting list, with each part's section, length and quantity. Find the material in the store and check that it is the right section and size, straight, and free of bad rust, pitting or damage. Plan the order of marking, and choose datums, such as one end and one edge, that all sizes will be measured from. Allow for the kerf, for bends, for weld shrinkage and for any machining. Collect the tools: tape and steel rule, square, scriber, soapstone or paint marker, centre punch and hammer, dividers or trammels, and templates, and check they are in good order, for example that the tape hook is not bent. Set the steel on firm trestles at a good working height, chocked so it cannot roll.
markingPoints: Reads the whole drawing, checks the revision and that the sizes add up; asks about anything unclear
Cutting list made or checked
Material checked for section, size, straightness and damage
Datums chosen and allowances (kerf, bends, shrinkage, machining) planned
Tools collected and checked; steel safely supported on chocked trestles

essays.stem: Describe five marking-out tools, say what each is used for, and how each one is kept accurate.
essays.modelAnswer: A tape measure is used for long measurements on plate and sections. Keep it accurate by checking that the hook is not bent or loose and by comparing it with a steel rule, and replace it if the blade is kinked. A steel rule measures shorter lengths and is used as a straight edge. Keep its edges and end free from dents, and do not use it as a scraper or a lever. An engineer's square is used to mark and check lines at 90° to an edge. Do not drop it, and check it now and then against a known square. A scriber scratches fine, lasting lines on clean or blued metal. Keep its point sharp and covered when it is not in use. A centre punch makes a dent so that the drill starts in the right place, and a dot punch makes light marks; keep their points ground to the right angle. Dividers and trammels scribe circles and arcs and step off distances. Keep their points sharp and their joints firm so they do not slip.
markingPoints: First correct tool and use, with how it is kept accurate
Second correct tool and use, with care
Third correct tool and use, with care
Fourth correct tool and use, with care
Fifth correct tool and use, with care

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to mark out a 300 mm × 200 mm base plate with four bolt holes 40 mm in from each edge, and how to check it.
essays.modelAnswer: Check the plate size and that two edges at one corner are straight and square, and mark them as the datum edges. Clean the surface and coat it with marking blue so that the lines show. Working from the datum edges with a steel rule, square and scriber, mark the outline of 300 mm × 200 mm if the plate is still to be cut. Check that the rectangle is square by measuring both diagonals: they should be equal, at about 361 mm. Next mark the hole centre lines: measure 40 mm in from each long edge and each short edge, and scribe the lines with the square. The hole centres are where these lines cross, so they are 220 mm apart along the length and 120 mm apart across the width. Check these distances, and check that the diagonals between the hole centres are equal, at about 251 mm. Dot punch lightly and check again, then centre punch the hole centres, scribe the hole circles with dividers and add witness marks. Mark the job and part number on the plate.
markingPoints: Datum edges checked straight and square; surface cleaned and blued
Outline marked from the datums and checked with equal diagonals (about 361 mm)
Hole centre lines 40 mm in from each edge (centres 220 mm and 120 mm apart)
Hole positions checked, including equal diagonals, before punching
Dot punch, check, centre punch; hole circles and witness marks scribed; part marked

essays.stem: Describe how to make a paper template for a 90° two-piece pipe mitre by parallel line development, and how to use it to mark the pipe.
essays.modelAnswer: A 90° two-piece mitre has each pipe cut at 45°. On paper, draw a side view of the pipe at full size, using its outside diameter, with the mitre line at 45° across one end. Draw a half circle on the end of the pipe view and divide it into six equal parts, which gives twelve parts round the full circle. Project lines from these points along the pipe to meet the mitre line. Next draw a straight stretch-out line equal to the outside circumference of the pipe (π × outside diameter), because the template will wrap around the outside. Divide it into twelve equal parts and draw a line up from each point. From where each projected line meets the mitre line, carry its height across to the matching line on the stretch-out. Join the points with a smooth curve and cut out the template. Mark the quarter lines on the pipe, wrap the template tightly around it, line its marks up with the quarter lines, and scribe or soapstone along the curve. Mark the waste side and the part number.
markingPoints: Full-size side view with the mitre line at 45°
End circle divided into equal parts (for example 12) and projected to the mitre line
Stretch-out equal to π × outside diameter, divided into the same number of parts
Heights transferred and joined with a smooth curve; template cut out
Template wrapped on the pipe, lined up with the quarter lines and marked; waste side marked

essays.stem: Describe how to mark out a length of channel for cutting to length and for drilling bolt holes in the web and the flanges.
essays.modelAnswer: Check the drawing for the length, the hole sizes, the pitch, the end distances and the back marks for the web and each flange. Check that the channel is straight and the right size. Square one end, or mark a square line near the end, to use as the datum. Measure the length along the back of the web from this datum, and carry a square cut line round the web and both flanges, checking that the lines meet. For the web holes, mark the hole lines along the web at the distances from the web edge that the drawing gives, then mark each hole from the datum end, measuring every hole from the datum rather than from hole to hole. For the flange holes, mark the back mark along each flange, measured from the back of the web, and mark the hole positions from the same datum end. Dot punch and check every position against the drawing, then centre punch and add witness marks. Mark the waste side of the cut line, and paint the part mark on the web.
markingPoints: Drawing checked for length, holes, pitch, end distances and back marks; channel checked
Square datum end; cut line carried square round the web and both flanges
Web hole lines and positions marked, each from the datum end
Flange holes marked on the back mark, measured from the back of the web
Positions checked, punched with witness marks; waste side and part mark shown

essays.stem: Explain how to develop the pattern for a cone frustum (a cone with its top cut off) using radial line development.
essays.modelAnswer: Draw the front view (elevation) of the frustum full size, or to scale, showing the large diameter at the bottom, the small diameter at the top and the height. Extend the two sloping sides upward until they meet at the apex of the full cone. Draw a half plan (a half circle) on the base and divide it into six equal parts, which gives twelve parts round the full base. On a clear part of the sheet, set the compass or trammels at the apex and draw an arc with a radius equal to the true slant length from the apex to the base. Draw a second arc from the same centre, with a radius equal to the slant length from the apex to the top of the frustum. Step off the twelve divisions of the base circle along the large arc, using the chord length from the plan. Join the first and last points back to the apex. The pattern is the shape between the two arcs and these two lines. Add a seam allowance if the job needs one, and cut it out.
markingPoints: Elevation drawn with the sides extended to meet at the apex
Base plan divided into equal parts (for example 12)
Arcs drawn from the apex with the slant lengths to the base and to the top
Base divisions stepped along the large arc; ends joined to the apex
Pattern is between the arcs; seam allowance added if needed

essays.stem: Explain how to make, check, label and use a template for marking out a batch of identical gusset plates.
essays.modelAnswer: Choose a template material that is stiff and will last for the number of parts, such as thin sheet steel, hardboard or heavy card. Mark the gusset shape on it accurately from the drawing, using a datum edge, a square and a rule, and include the hole centres. Cut it out carefully and file the edges smooth and straight. Drill or punch small holes at the hole centres so that a scriber or punch can be used through them. Check the template against the drawing, measuring every size, angle and hole position, and ask the supervisor to check it too. Label it clearly with the job number, part number, quantity, material thickness and date, and show which side is up. To use it, place it on clean plate in the position that wastes least material, hold or clamp it firmly, and mark round it with a scriber or soapstone, allowing for the kerf. Mark the hole centres through the template holes. Check the first part made against the drawing, and store the template flat after use.
markingPoints: Suitable stiff template material chosen
Shape and hole centres marked accurately from a datum; cut and filed; holes made for marking through
Template checked against the drawing, and by the supervisor
Labelled with job, part number, quantity, thickness and date
Used clamped on the plate to save material, kerf allowed, hole centres marked; first part checked; stored flat

essays.stem: Explain the main causes of errors in marking out, and how to avoid each of them.
essays.modelAnswer: Errors add up when each size is measured from the last mark. Avoid this by measuring every size from one datum line or edge. A datum edge that is not straight or square throws every mark off, so check the datum edge first with a straight edge and a square. Faulty tools give wrong sizes: a tape with a bent or loose hook, a worn rule or a square that has been dropped. Check tools before use and replace damaged ones. Parallax error comes from looking at the rule from an angle, so always look straight down at the mark. Thick or unclear lines make it hard to cut accurately, so use marking blue and a sharp scriber on clean metal, or a fine soapstone line on rough plate. Misreading the drawing, or using an old revision, makes whole parts wrong, so check the drawing number and revision and ask when something is unclear. Forgetting allowances for the kerf, bends or weld shrinkage gives parts that are the wrong size. Finally, check the job again before it is cut.
markingPoints: Errors adding up — measure everything from one datum
Datum edge not straight or square — check it first
Faulty tools (tape hook, worn rule, dropped square) — check and replace
Parallax and unclear lines — look straight down; fine, clear lines on clean or blued metal
Wrong drawing or missed allowances — check the revision, allow for kerf and bends, recheck before cutting

essays.stem: Explain why allowances are needed when marking out, such as for the kerf, bending, machining and weld shrinkage, and how each one affects your marks.
essays.modelAnswer: The drawing shows the finished size of a part, but some processes add or remove metal, so the marks must allow for them. Kerf: a flame, plasma or saw cut removes a strip of metal. Mark the finished line and cut on the waste side of it, or mark the cut line half a kerf away, so that the part is not undersize. Bending: when plate or sheet is bent, the outside stretches and the inside squeezes, so the flat length is worked out at the neutral axis, for example using the mean diameter for a rolled cylinder. The bend lines are marked from this length, not from the outside sizes. Machining or grinding: if an edge is to be machined or ground, extra metal is left on, often a few millimetres, so the cut line is marked further out. Weld shrinkage: welds shrink as they cool and pull the parts closer, so some jobs are marked slightly long or with a gap allowance, as the drawing or supervisor says. Write the allowances on the cutting list so that they are not forgotten.
markingPoints: The drawing shows finished sizes; processes add or remove metal
Kerf — cut on the waste side or offset the line
Bending — flat length worked out at the neutral axis (mean diameter for cylinders); bend lines marked from it
Machining — extra metal left, cut line marked further out
Weld shrinkage — marked slightly long or with a gap as instructed; allowances recorded

essays.stem: Describe the safety hazards when marking out structural steel, how to control them, and how to care for the tools at the end of the job.
essays.modelAnswer: Heavy steel sections and plates can crush hands and feet or strain the back. Use lifting equipment or enough people to lift, wear safety boots and gloves, and set the steel on firm trestles, chocked so it cannot roll or tip. Sharp edges, burrs and slivers on cut steel can cut the hands, so wear gloves and deburr edges where needed. Punching and hammering can make chips fly into the eyes, so wear safety glasses and use a hammer with a sound handle. Scriber, divider and trammel points can stab, so keep them covered and carry them pointing down. Tape blades can cut fingers when they snap back, so let them return slowly. Marking fluids and paint markers give off fumes, so use them with good ventilation and keep them capped. Steel, offcuts and tools left on the floor cause trips, so keep the area clear. At the end of the job, wipe the tools clean, oil steel tools lightly against rust, cover sharp points, check for damage, report any faults, and return the tools to their places.
markingPoints: Heavy steel: lifting aids or a team lift, boots, firm chocked trestles
Sharp edges and burrs: gloves and deburring
Flying chips: safety glasses and a sound hammer; sharp points covered
Other hazards controlled: tape snap-back, fumes from marking fluids, trips
Tools cleaned, lightly oiled, points covered, checked, faults reported, put away

practical1.title: Mark out a base plate with bolt holes on a rectangle and on a pitch circle
practical1.brief: Each member of the group marks out one base plate on a piece of 6–10 mm mild steel plate about 250 mm × 250 mm, from the instructor's drawing. Check and mark two datum edges, blue the surface, and mark: the outline and centre lines; four corner holes 30 mm in from each edge; a 150 mm pitch circle with six holes evenly spaced on it; and a 60 mm centre hole circle. Dot punch, check, then centre punch every hole centre and add witness marks. Members then swap plates and check each other's work against the drawing, measuring the diagonals and the hole spacings and writing the results on a check sheet. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with every member's plate and the check sheets.
materials: One piece of 6–10 mm mild steel plate, about 250 mm × 250 mm, for each member
Marking blue, scriber, and soapstone or a paint marker
Steel rule, tape measure, engineer's square and combination set
Dividers, dot punch, centre punch and hammer
The instructor's drawing and a check sheet
photos: Each plate with the datum edges marked and the surface blued
The outline and centre lines scribed
The corner hole centres marked, with the diagonals being measured
The pitch circle scribed and the six holes being stepped off
The punched centres with witness marks (close-up)
Every member's finished plate laid out together, with the check sheets
checklist: Checked and marked two datum edges, and blued a clean surface
Measured every size from the datums, not from mark to mark
Corner holes within about 1 mm of 30 mm from each edge, with equal diagonals
Six holes evenly spaced on the 150 mm pitch circle, stepped off at the radius (75 mm)
Dot punched, checked, then centre punched neatly, with witness marks
Lines fine and clear, with the job and part number marked
Checked another member's plate correctly and recorded the results
Wore safety glasses when punching, and left the tools clean and put away
safety: Wear safety glasses when punching; use a hammer with a sound, tight head
Wear gloves when handling plate; the edges may be sharp
Keep scriber and divider points covered when not in use
Use marking blue with good ventilation and keep it capped

practical2.title: Develop a paper template for a 90° two-piece pipe mitre and mark it onto steel pipe
practical2.brief: Each member of the group develops, by parallel line development, a full-size paper template for one half of a 90° two-piece mitre on a mild steel pipe of the size the instructor gives (about 60–90 mm outside diameter). Measure the pipe, draw the side view with the 45° mitre line, divide the end circle into 12 equal parts, draw the stretch-out (π × outside diameter) and plot the curve. Cut out the template, mark the quarter lines on a length of pipe, wrap the template round it, and mark the cut line with a scriber or soapstone, showing the waste side. Members check each other's templates by wrapping them on the pipe: the ends should meet exactly. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with every member's template and marked pipe.
materials: Steel pipe, about 60–90 mm outside diameter, one length of about 300 mm for each member
Drawing paper or thin card, longer than the pipe's distance round
Drawing instruments: rule, set squares, compass or dividers, protractor
Vernier caliper or tape to measure the pipe
Scissors, scriber, soapstone and a wraparound strip
A firm bench, or pipe vee blocks to stop the pipe rolling
photos: The pipe being measured, with the outside diameter written down
The side view with the 45° mitre line and the divided end circle
The stretch-out with the plotted points and the curve
The cut-out template wrapped on the pipe, lined up with the quarter lines
The cut line marked on the pipe, with the waste side shown
Every member's template and marked pipe laid out together
checklist: Measured the pipe accurately and worked out the stretch-out length correctly
Drew the side view and the 45° mitre line accurately
Divided the circle and the stretch-out into the same number of equal parts
Transferred the heights and drew a smooth, accurate curve
Template wraps the pipe with its ends meeting, lined up with the quarter lines
Marked a clear cut line and showed the waste side
Supported the pipe so it could not roll, and kept the area tidy
safety: Chock the pipe or use vee blocks so it cannot roll off the bench
Wear gloves when handling cut pipe; the ends may be sharp
Keep scriber and divider points covered when not in use
Use scissors and knives carefully, cutting away from the body
